home.designation: Former Parliament Member & former Education Minister
home.intro: Shisir Khanal co-founded Teach For Nepal, which has placed hundreds of fellows in the country's most underserved classrooms. His path to politics ran through the Sarvodaya Shramdan movement, where he led reconstruction efforts in Sri Lanka and Haiti before returning home to build. He studied public policy at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
home.parliamentHighlight1Description: 15+ parliamentary interventions and ₹100+ crore directed to local infrastructure your concerns raised at the national level.
home.parliamentHighlight2Description: 367 days on the ground turned local issues into national priorities.
home.parliamentHighlight3Title: Serious Policy Work Happens in Committees
home.parliamentHighlight3Description: Leading studies, reviewing bills, and proposing reforms where real decisions are made.
home.ministerHighlight1Description: Remote districts received books before the school year started a historic first for Nepal.
home.ministerHighlight2Description: The NOC process for students streamlined with data, clear goals, and rapid execution.
home.ministerHighlight3Description: Clear priorities, tight coordination, and rapid sprints delivered measurable change in just 19 days.
home.ktmHighlight1Description: 15+ interventions on water, roads, and public land local problems put on the national record.
home.ktmHighlight2Description: Roads, water systems, and public works pushed forward through budget advocacy.
home.ktmHighlight3Description: Issues recorded, ministries questioned, and pressure maintained for solutions.

about.bioP1: My childhood moved with my father's civil service postings—Tanahun, Mustang, Chitwan, eventually Kathmandu. That kind of upbringing shows you Nepal in full: the richness of its communities, but also how uneven opportunity is spread across them.
about.bioP2: I studied public policy at UW-Madison, always with the intention of bringing that training home. But before returning, I spent several years with the Sarvodaya Shramadana movement, the Gandhian community development network active across South Asia. The work took me to Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami and to Haiti after the 2010 earthquake—both times working alongside communities rebuilding on their own terms. I wasn't there as an expert. I was learning what it actually takes to make institutions serve people instead of failing them.
about.bioP3: After moving back to Nepal, I co-founded Teach For Nepal in 2012 with a small group of friends who shared a frustration of talented young Nepalis having few pathways into public service, and the schools that needed them most were invisible to the system. We started with 33 fellows in 16 schools. The organization has since placed hundreds of graduates in underserved classrooms across the country—some stayed in education, others carried the experience into government, health, business, and elsewhere.
about.bioP4: I also started PickNDrop, a logistics company that now employs more than 50 people. When the 2015 earthquake struck, I helped coordinate relief in affected communities. When COVID-19 closed schools in 2020, we piloted "टोल-टोलमा सिकाई" in Tulsipur—neighborhood learning circles that kept children studying when classrooms were inaccessible. That model later informed national education policy.
about.bioP5: In 2022, voters in Kathmandu-6 elected me to Parliament. I served briefly as Minister of Education, Science and Technology, where my team addressed the chronic textbook shortage in public schools and reduced NOC processing from 75 days to less than a week.
about.bioP6: Politics isn't a career for me. The only question I'm interested in is whether it can be made to build things that last.

work.transparencyDescription: Every issue I raise in parliament is backed by research and constituent feedback. The government must answer to the people, not through rhetoric, but through documented questions and persistent follow-up.
work.communityToParliamentDescription: 367 days in the constituency over three years were spent listening. Those conversations became parliamentary interventions. Kathmandu-6's water crisis, road conditions, and public land issues are now on the national record. They have been raised 15+ times in Zero Hour, backed by written questions, and supported by formal resolutions. ₹100 crore+ has been directed to constituency infrastructure development.
work.researchBackedDescription: I serve on the Foreign Relations and International Trade Committee. I led the Nepal Airlines Corporation Study Sub-Committee. I review bills, propose amendments, and draft private member bills. Speaking in parliament is not enough. The work is in studying policy, consulting experts, and proposing solutions that can actually be implemented.
work.coalitionBuildingDescription: Parliament works when members collaborate across party lines. I have jointly filed resolutions with MPs from other parties, coordinated on shared concerns, and led dialogue teams for political alliances. Results require coalition, not confrontation.
work.zeroHourSummary: I have raised issues in Zero Hour 15+ times

work.parliamentToolForChange: Parliament is a tool for change. Every question raised, every committee meeting, every coalition built serves one purpose: translate Kathmandu-6's voices into national action.
work.ministerHeroDescription:
I served as Minister of Education, Science and Technology for 19 days. Short, yes. But enough to demonstrate what capable leadership with clear priorities can achieve.
This was not symbolic or ritualistic work. These were structural changes requiring coordination with bureaucracy, navigating supply chain bottlenecks, and solving problems that had persisted for years.
work.ministerAction1Title: 1. For the First Time in Nepal’s history, Textbooks were supplied on time
work.ministerAction1P1: For the first time, remote districts from Humla to Taplejug received textbooks before the academic year started.
work.ministerAction1P2: Humla, a Himalayan district that routinely received books months late—sometimes after annual exams—had textbooks delivered before Baisakh 1.
work.ministerAction1Requirement1: Coordination across Ministry, Curriculum Development Center, publishers, and transporters
work.ministerAction1Requirement2: Addressing supply chain issues specific to remote areas (air transport unreliability, road accessibility)
work.ministerAction1Requirement3: Budget release synchronization with local governments
work.ministerAction1P3: This wasn't about issuing directives. It was about understanding where the system was breaking and fixing those specific points.
work.ministerAction1P4: As a result of this, students in Humla's and other remote districts’ community schools had books on day one. A historic first.
work.ministerAction2P1: Students seeking No Objection Certificates to study abroad were stuck in a 75-day bureaucratic maze. Multiple office visits. Unclear timelines. Uncertainty.
work.ministerAction2P2: We reduced this to under 5 days.
work.ministerAction2P3: We didn't start with software. We started with understanding the problem.
work.ministerWeek1Description: We Interviewed students. Mapped their actual journey—from decision to study abroad to departure. Identified pain points in this journey.
work.ministerWeek2Description: Met with ministry officials. Presented data, not anecdotes. Showed them what students were experiencing on the ground. Aligned everyone around a citizen-centric approach.
work.ministerWeek3Goal1: Reduce in-person office visits from 100% to 40%
work.ministerWeek3Goal2: Reduce processing time to under 5 days for 80% of applicants
work.ministerAction2P4: Replaced one-year planning cycles with two-week sprints. Established a team. Assigned clear tasks. Build accountability through simple tracking tools.
work.ministerAction2P5: The insight: Most public service failures aren't about bad software or inadequate budget. They're about broken processes and misaligned priorities. Fix those first.
work.ministerAction2P6:
The result: First sprint completed. Goals on track. Students no longer traveling to Kathmandu for multiple office visits.
(Implementation credit: Digital transformation work led with Kailash Badu)
work.whyThisMattersIntro: These are examples of what's possible when you:
work.whyThisMattersPoint1: Start with the citizen's experience, not the bureaucracy's convenience
work.whyThisMattersPoint2: Use data to understand problems, not assumptions
work.whyThisMattersPoint3: Coordinate across systems, not just issue orders
work.whyThisMattersP1: Nepal's education system has hundreds of such problems. Low-hanging fruit that requires capable execution, not grand visions.
work.whyThisMattersP2: There are dozens more like these. They don't require massive budgets. They require leadership that understands how systems work and how to make them work for people.
work.whatILearnedP1: Ministries are not stages for speeches. They are tools for change.
work.whatILearnedP2: 19 days proved that with clear priorities, coordination skills, and bias for action, real problems can be solved quickly.
work.whatILearnedP3: The question is: do we want leaders who know how to do this work, or leaders who only know how to talk about it?
work.voicesRaisedP1: 15+ times your issues were raised in Zero Hour and written questions.
work.voicesRaisedP2: Water: Dharmasthali, Phutung, Manmaiju, Nepal Taar, Samakhusi, Gongabu—demanded solutions for areas Melamchi doesn't reach
work.voicesRaisedP3: Roads: Chakrapath expansion, Nepal Taar-Dadagaun, Sangla Bihani, Thamel-Gongabu—raised repeatedly, filed joint resolution
work.voicesRaisedP4: Public Land: Tarkeshwar 9 encroachment, Judicial Academy area issues
work.voicesRaisedP5: Other: Gongabu bus park vandalism, Bagmati construction zone concerns
work.voicesRaisedP6: Problems documented. Government questioned. Solutions demanded.
work.resourcesMobilizedP2: Roads, water projects, public infrastructure—mobilized through constituency development programs and budget advocacy.
work.communityWorkP1: 367+ days in the constituency. Ward-level hearings, project monitoring, school visits, grievance redressal.
work.communityWorkP2: The issues raised in parliament came from listening to you.
work.whatsNextPoint1: The problems are known. The work has started. Evidence is there.
work.whatsNextPoint2: Now this work needs to continue.
